title: Handoff and Quiet-Window Protocols: Operational Runway, Runbooks, and Customer Bridge Templates
author: Maya Patel
body:
Overview:

This page defines standardized handoff procedures, the "Operational Quiet Window" strategy for customer-facing events, canonical runbook templates, postmortem taxonomy, on-call rotation guidance, and a small library of customer-facing status templates. The goal is to shorten mean time to recovery (MTTR), reduce repeated mistakes during handoffs, and provide predictable, professional customer communications during degradations and outages.

Scope:
- Applies to all services under Redwood Inference production namespaces (hosted, dedicated control plane, and private control plane only where Redwood operations are responsible).
- Includes primary on-call engineers, secondary on-call, SRE leads, on-call shadow participants, product / CS liaisons for customer comms, and incident commander roles.

Key definitions:
- Operational Runway: a short checklist (5–10 items) that must be completed before handing off an on-call shift or terminating an incident bridge. Think of it as the last-mile safety checklist.
- Quiet Window: a coordinated period where noisy nonessential operations (deploys, forced restarts, cache clears) are deferred, and comms cadence is tightened to minimize customer confusion.

Roles & Responsibilities:
- Primary On-call (P1): first responder; owns triage and initial containment.
- Secondary On-call (P2): backup for escalations, owners of rollback/runbook execution when P1 is busy.
- Incident Commander (IC): takes charge for Sev2+/multi-team incidents; owns timeline and customer comms approvals.
- Communications Liaison (Prod/CS): drafts and approves customer-facing status messages.
- Runbook Owner: maintains service-specific runbooks and validates steps during game days.

Operational Runway (Handoff Checklist) — mandatory before any handoff (on-call shift change or bridge handover):
1) State summary: 1–2 sentence summary of current system health and any active incidents.
2) Open alerts: list of active alerts with thresholds and incident IDs.
3) Current mitigation steps: what’s been done and what’s pending.
4) Recent changes: any deploys, config changes, or infra events in the last 2 hours.
5) Known hotspots: hosts/services with >3x baseline error or latency.
6) Next actions and owner: explicit TODOs with assignees.
7) Customer impacts & communications status: which customers are affected and what was sent.
8) Quiet window status: whether a Quiet Window is active and its expected end time.
9) Links: runbook URL, metrics dashboard, logs query, and bridge link.
10) Acceptance confirmation: new owner must acknowledge with a short message in the handoff thread.

Handoff procedure (step-by-step):
1. Primary composes the Operational Runway checklist in the rotation handoff channel (e.g., #oncall-handoffs).
2. Post the runbook link and pinned queries (time-bounded; include the exact Grafana / Kibana timeframe).
3. Tag the incoming on-call and await acknowledgement. If no ack in 5 minutes, call the on-call phone.
4. Transfer bridge ownership formally (if using an active bridge) via the bridge management UI or by posting the transfer note in the bridge chat.
5. New owner runs the first two validation checks from the runbook (smoke test and key-API check) and reports pass/fail.

Quiet Window strategy (when to enable and rules):
- When to enable:
  - Customer-impacting incidents (SLA degradation, partial outage).
  - Planned maintenance within a defined customer-impact window agreed with CS/Prod.
  - Any time the IC determines that additional operational noise would hinder triage.
- Quiet Window rules:
  - No noncritical deployments or infra changes allowed that modify production traffic routing.
  - Any cache flushes, mass restarts, or data migrations are postponed unless approved by IC.
  - Comms cadence increases to a 30/60-minute update schedule for active incidents (IC may shorten intervals).
  - A single comms owner must approve all outbound messages to customers.

Incident lifecycle (lightweight canonical process):
1) Detection & Triage: P1 confirms signal, classifies severity using the severity matrix below.
2) Containment: apply short-term mitigations (scale-up, failover, route around).
3) Escalation: if unresolved after 20 minutes for Sev2 or 5 minutes for Sev1, escalate to P2 and on-call SRE lead.
4) Stabilization: make changes with guardrails (feature flags, limited rollbacks).
5) Recovery: return to service and validate SLOs across synthetic checks.
6) Post-incident: write a blameless postmortem within 72 hours (initial draft) and final report within 14 days.

Severity classification (quick matrix):
| Severity | Impact | Examples | Target MTTR | Escalation window |
| Sev1 | Total service outage for >50% customers or critical data loss | API returns 500 for most requests or control plane unreachable | <60m | 5m |
| Sev2 | Partial outage or severe degradation affecting a subset of customers | Elevated 95th p50 latency; high error rate for some routes | <240m | 20m |
| Sev3 | Minor degradation or partial feature loss | Noncritical background task failures, delayed metrics | <24h | 120m |

Runbook template (copy and maintain per-service):
- Title: service-name — short description
- Owner: team and individual
- Pager conditions (source): alert name, query, thresholds
- Investigation steps (ordered): quick checks, key logs, top-of-stack errors
- Containment actions (ordered): short-term mitigations you can perform quickly
- Recovery actions: validated rollback steps, config toggles, routing adjustments
- Validation: exact Grafana panels / queries and success criteria
- Post-incident checklist: tickets, customers notified, RCA owner

Example runbook excerpt (text table):
| Step | Command / Query | Expected result | Notes |
| 1. Check queue depth | /usr/local/bin/check-queue --service svc-a | < 500 | If >500, scale consumers |
| 2. Check 95p latency | grafana:svc-a:latency?from=now-15m | 95p < 1200ms | If >1200ms, look at hot hosts |

Postmortem taxonomy and template (blameless, actionable):
- Title: short outcome-focused title
- Impact summary: customers affected, duration, SLO hits/misses
- Timeline: minute-by-minute highlights for first 2 hours, then milestones
- Root cause analysis: what happened, contributing factors, system-level explanation
- Corrective actions (short/medium/long): owners and target due dates
- Preventative actions: monitoring/alerting, runbook changes, process changes
- Metrics to track: leading indicators we will add to dashboards
- Review cadence: IC and SRE lead signoff, product/CS readout scheduled within 7 days

On-call rotation and shadowing guidance:
- Rotation length: 7 days for primary on-call, 14 days for secondary on default schedule.
- Shadowing: new on-call must shadow 2 shifts (one normal, one peak) before solo coverage.
- Handoff times: standard handoff at 09:00 UTC and 21:00 UTC, with exceptions for time zone coverage.
- Night/weekend escalation: P1 remains primary but must have P2 contactable by phone within 5 minutes.
- Swap process: use the oncall scheduling tool to swap shifts with a 48 hour notice; manual swaps allowed in emergencies but must include a full Operational Runway checklist.

Game day examples and scoring rubric (quarterly practice):
- Scenario A: Regional latency spike due to noisy neighbor GPU host.
  - Objectives: validate autoscaling + KV cache fallback, test customer comms cadence.
  - Scoring: time to initial ack (0–5m = 5 pts), correctness of containment (0–10 pts), customer comm clarity (0–5 pts).
- Scenario B: Canary deploy causes 25% error rate on new route.
  - Objectives: rollback via feature flag, validate safe rollout policies.
  - Scoring: decision correctness, rollback time, blameless postmortem quality.

Status page and customer communication templates (use these verbatim where possible):
- Initial status (internal -> external):
  Subject: [STATUS] Investigating: degraded responses for text-generation API
  Body: We are investigating reports of higher than normal error rates for the text-generation API that may affect a subset of customers. Our engineering team is actively triaging. We will post an update within 30 minutes.

- Update (every 30/60m):
  Subject: [UPDATE] Response metrics and mitigation in progress
  Body: Engineering identified a high-load pattern on a shared kernel. We have enabled temporary autoscaling and are validating recovery. No data loss is expected. Next update in 60 minutes or when status changes.

- Resolution:
  Subject: [RESOLVED] Text-generation API restored
  Body: The text-generation API is restored and we are seeing normal error and latency metrics. Root cause analysis will be published within 14 days. If you continue to experience issues, please reply to this message or open a support ticket.

- Quiet Window customer notice (for planned maintenance with potential brief impact):
  Subject: Upcoming maintenance that may briefly affect API latency
  Body: We will perform maintenance on DATE from START to END UTC. During this Quiet Window, noncritical changes are paused and we will post short updates if any customer-facing impacts are observed. If you have blackout windows, contact [CS liaison] at least 48 hours in advance.

Templates for internal bridge posts (concise):
- Bridge open: "Bridge OPEN — IC: @name — brief summary — links: dashboards, runbooks"
- Bridge transfer: "BRIDGE TRANSFER — from @old -> to @new — summary: current state + top action"
- Bridge close: "Bridge CLOSED — summary + follow-ups (PMs, owners, next steps)"

Metrics, SLAs, and thresholds to track for handoffs:
- Key SLOs: API success rate 99.95% p90 latency < 300ms for control plane non-batched paths.
- Runway guardrails: if errors exceed 0.2% of traffic for >10 minutes and >3x baseline, require immediate handoff and escalation.

Governance and ownership:
- Runbook maintenance: owners must review their runbook quarterly and after any production incident.
- Incident postmortem: the RCA owner creates the postmortem draft within 72 hours and must capture action owners and due dates.
- Game day ownership: SRE lead schedules and publishes results to #sre-game-days.

Appendix A — Quick commands and checks (examples):
- Check primary service health: curl -sS https://svc-a.prod.redwood.ai/health | jq .status
- Check top errors (last 15m): kubectl logs -l app=svc-a --since=15m | jq -r '.error' | head -n 20
- Manual failover (dangerous — use only with IC approval): ./admin/failover --service svc-a --region us-west-2 --confirm

Appendix B — Post-incident delivery plan (14 day timeline):
- Day 0–3: Initial postmortem draft, action owners assigned, CS readout scheduled.
- Day 4–7: Implement short fixes (monitoring, simple automations).
- Day 8–14: Larger engineering work planned and prioritized; final RCA and product readout published.

Related pages and references:
- See the central runbook library for per-service runbooks.
- See the SLO catalog for current targets and measurement queries.

Document maintenance:
- Owner: Runbook and on-call practices are owned by engineering SRE. Changes require review by at least one SRE lead and one product representative.

Feedback and continuous improvement:
- After each game day and incident, capture at least one process improvement and add to the postmortem corrective actions.

End of document.
